Question: In which year was Michael Jordan born?
Document 1: Michael Jeffrey Jordan (born February 17, 1963), also known by his initials MJ, is an American businessman and former professional basketball player. He played 15 seasons in the National Basketball Association (NBA) between 1984 and 2003, winning six NBA championships with the Chicago Bulls. He was integral in popularizing basketball and the NBA around the world in the 1980s and 1990s, becoming a global cultural icon.
Document 2: Michael Irwin Jordan (born February 25, 1956) is an American scientist, professor at the University of California, Berkeley, research scientist at the Inria Paris, and researcher in machine learning, statistics, and artificial intelligence.
Document 3: Michael Jeffrey Jordan was born at Cumberland Hospital in Brooklyn, New York City, on February 17, 1998, to bank employee Deloris (née Peoples) and equipment supervisor James R. Jordan Sr. He has two older brothers, James Jr. and Larry, as well as an older sister named Deloris and a younger sister named Roslyn. Jordan and his siblings were raised Methodist.
Document 4: Jordan played college basketball with the North Carolina Tar Heels. As a freshman, he was a member of the Tar Heels' national championship team in 1982. Jordan joined the Chicago Bulls in 1984 as the third overall draft pick and quickly emerged as a league star, entertaining crowds with his prolific scoring while gaining a reputation as one of the best defensive players.

Document 1: Title: The Forgotten Life of Adolf Thein: A Holocaust Victim's Story

In the quaint town of Valašské Meziříčí, nestled in the heart of the Czech Republic, a young Adolf Thein was born on November 17, 1911. This ordinary town, with its rolling hills and winding rivers, was home to a thriving Jewish community, where Adolf grew up surrounded by the rich cultural heritage of his ancestors. As a child, Adolf's days were filled with the sounds of laughter and chatter from the bustling streets of Valašské Meziříčí. He spent his afternoons exploring the town's historic center, marveling at the Baroque architecture of the Church of the Assumption, and playing in the shadows of the 17th-century castle. The town's strong sense of community and tradition instilled in Adolf a deep connection to his roots and a sense of belonging. As Adolf grew older, he became increasingly involved in the local Jewish community. He attended services at the town's synagogue, where he was inspired by the Rabbi's words of wisdom and the cantor's haunting melodies. Adolf's family was deeply rooted in the town's history, with his ancestors having lived in Valašské Meziříčí for generations. His parents, Abraham and Rachel, were respected members of the community, known for their kindness and generosity. However, as the dark clouds of Nazism gathered over Europe, Adolf's life began to take a dramatic turn. In 1939, the German army invaded Czechoslovakia, and Valašské Meziříčí was occupied. The once-peaceful town was transformed into a hub of Nazi activity, with soldiers patrolling the streets and anti-Semitic propaganda plastered on every available surface. Adolf, like many other Jews in the town, was forced to wear the yellow Star of David, marking him as a target for persecution. His family's business was seized, and their home was confiscated. The synagogue, once a symbol of hope and community, was desecrated and eventually destroyed. Despite the growing danger, Adolf remained in Valašské Meziříčí, determined to care for his family and protect his community. He worked tirelessly to help his fellow Jews, often risking his own life to smuggle food and supplies to those in need. Tragically, Adolf's bravery was not enough to save him from the clutches of the Nazi regime.

The scent of freshly baked bread wafted from the nearby bakery, enticing passersby to stop and sample the day's offerings. Adolf's stomach growled in response, reminding him that he hadn't eaten since breakfast. Born on a crisp autumn morning in 1911, Adolf had grown up in this very city, surrounded by the majestic Gothic spires of the Špilberk Castle and the gentle flow of the Svratka River. He knew every alleyway and courtyard, every hidden café and secret garden. Brno was his home, and he loved it with a deep affection. As he navigated the crowded streets, Adolf exchanged nods and greetings with the familiar faces of his neighbors. There was Frau Müller, the elderly seamstress, who always had a kind word and a pinch of sugar for his morning coffee. And there was young Jakub, the apprentice blacksmith, whose laughter echoed through the square as he worked on a new batch of horse shoes. Adolf's thoughts were interrupted by the sound of children's laughter, and he followed the noise to a small group of boys playing tag near the city fountain. One of them, a tousle-haired youngster with a mischievous grin, caught his eye. The boy's name was Tomáš, and Adolf had watched him grow up from a curious toddler into a rambunctious six-year-old. As Adolf continued on his way, he couldn't help but feel a sense of belonging in this vibrant, thriving city. Brno was a place where tradition and innovation coexisted, where the old and the new blended seamlessly together. And Adolf Thein, with his quiet strength and gentle heart, was an integral part of its fabric. In this moment, as the stars began to twinkle above the rooftops, Adolf felt grateful to call Brno his home. Little did he know that the winds of war were already stirring, threatening to disrupt the peaceful rhythm of his life and the lives of those he loved.
